results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: the prerequisite idea, what the topic is, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

h2_headings: before we start: what is a large language model?

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.
evidence: (31 words) The LLM generates the final answer: "The fine for returning a library book late is ten rupees per day." It adds that this is according to page 12 of your rulebook.
results.fix: Split every sentence longer than 25 words into two or three short sentences. One idea per sentence.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 850 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: Verified links to learn more
results.criterion: A 'Learn more' section links 2-4 resources, at least one a video, and EVERY link in the lesson is on the list verified live during research (no invented or broken URLs).

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (a misconception from the reference sheet, even softened, is a FAIL).
results.reasoning: Every technical claim and statement in the lesson was verified against the reference facts and misconception guidelines. All facts align correctly with the reference sheet, and none of the prohibited misconceptions are present. The absolute claims regarding limits are fully supported and consistent. Every required statement was verified against the reference text and found to be accurately quoted verbatim from the lesson content without containing false or misleading claims or promoting any known misconceptions. I checked every required definition and technical claim in the lesson against the reference facts and misconceptions list. All definitions match the reference facts precisely, and no listed misconceptions or false claims appear anywhere in the text.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: I checked all nine must-cover points in the reference list against the lesson content. Every point, including LLM limitations, the breakdown of RAG, why it matters, the technical preparation steps, retrieval, augmentation, generation, system limits, and a realistic use case, is thoroughly explained with direct supporting text.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
evidence: 'prompt' is explained in simple words at or before its FIRST use in the body. AUTOMATIC PRE-CHECK found no explanation in the sentence of first use: "Prompt augmentation: The system places the retrieved text pieces into the prompt along with the user's question.". Mark met=true ONLY if you can quote an earlier explanation. -> "(no proof: quote not found in the lesson) Seventh, prompt augmentation means placing the retrieved text pieces into the instructions along with the user's question."
results.fix: Fix each unmet item listed in the evidence.
results.reasoning: I checked every technical and uncommon term in the lesson against the criteria. All terms, including acronyms and conceptual jargon, are properly introduced, expanded, and explained in simple terms either right before or immediately at their first use.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to the topic, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single case through every step the lesson lists under 'How does it work?', in order, to its result.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy, its mapping, and a single worked example following every step in the 'How does it work?' section. All requirements are fully satisfied with clear quotes from the text.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: The lesson uses simple, accessible English appropriate for a non-native beginner. It avoids idioms, slang, and complex grammatical structures while explicitly explaining all technical terms like embeddings and vector indices. The tone is encouraging, directly addressing the learner using 'you'.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for section order, term introduction, section transitions, and purposeful repetition/analogies. All sections follow the exact requested sequence. Terms like embedding are defined when introduced, transitions between sections feel natural, and analogies (like the open-book exam and the student) are well-placed.

change_log.change: Split long compound sentences about the open-book exam and the final LLM answer into multiple short sentences under 25 words.
Expanded the worked example section to explicitly list all eight steps from document collection to generation in order.
